subChunks.title: Tailwind Config Deep-Dive
subChunks.hookHtml: Tailwind v4 replaced tailwind.config.js with a CSS-first configuration system. Your design tokens live in CSS, not JavaScript — and everything you define automatically becomes a Tailwind utility. This is where a generic framework becomes your design system.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Grand Archmage Solomon's study is colder than the rest of the tower. He sets down a quill and slides a CSS file across the desk without looking up.

Grand Archmage Solomon: "In the old days, apprentices wrestled with JavaScript config files. Tailwind v4 put the tokens where they belong — in CSS itself. The system is simpler and far more powerful. Sit. We begin."

@theme — the constitution

Every token you define in an @theme block becomes a CSS variable and a Tailwind utility automatically. Define a colour once, get bg-brand, text-brand, border-brand, and every other variant for free.

/* index.css */
@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  /* Colors */
  --color-brand:     oklch(0.55 0.20 270);   /* bg-brand, text-brand, etc. */
  --color-brand-50:  oklch(0.97 0.02 270);
  --color-brand-100: oklch(0.93 0.05 270);
  --color-brand-600: oklch(0.55 0.20 270);
  --color-brand-900: oklch(0.25 0.10 270);

  /* Typography */
  --font-display: "Cal Sans", sans-serif;    /* font-display */
  --font-mono:    "JetBrains Mono", monospace;

  /* Spacing */
  --spacing-18: 4.5rem;   /* p-18, m-18, w-18, gap-18 */
  --spacing-88: 22rem;

  /* Breakpoints */
  --breakpoint-xs:  480px;   /* xs:text-sm, xs:flex, etc. */
  --breakpoint-3xl: 1920px;

  /* Radius & shadow */
  --radius-4xl: 2rem;
  --shadow-glow: 0 0 20px 4px oklch(0.55 0.2 270 / 0.4);
}

The naming convention is always --{category}-{name}. Tailwind reads the category to know which utilities to generate. --color-* → colour utilities. --spacing-* → spacing utilities. --font-* → font-family utilities.

The semantic token pattern — how theming survives a rebrand

The real power of @theme is combining it with CSS variable overrides for dark mode and white-label theming:

@import "tailwindcss";
@variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *));

@theme {
  /* Semantic tokens — these map to design intent, not colours */
  --color-primary:            var(--color-brand-600);
  --color-primary-foreground: oklch(0.99 0 0);
  --color-surface:            oklch(0.99 0 0);
  --color-foreground:         oklch(0.15 0 0);
}

/* Dark mode overrides the same variable names */
.dark {
  --color-primary:            var(--color-brand-400);
  --color-surface:            oklch(0.12 0 0);
  --color-foreground:         oklch(0.95 0 0);
}

/* White-label client? Change four variables, not thousands of classes. */
.theme-emerald {
  --color-brand-600: oklch(0.53 0.17 155);
  --color-brand-400: oklch(0.72 0.15 155);
}
<!-- Usage is identical regardless of theme -->
<button class="bg-primary text-primary-foreground hover:bg-primary/90">
  Save
</button>

Flipping dark mode = one class toggle on <html>. Rebranding = changing the brand colour variables. The utility classes never change.

Custom utilities: @utility

/* Define a custom utility that Tailwind treats as a first-class citizen */
@utility scrollbar-hide {
  -ms-overflow-style: none;
  scrollbar-width: none;
  &::-webkit-scrollbar { display: none; }
}

@utility focus-ring {
  outline: 2px solid var(--color-primary);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

/* Usage: same as any built-in utility, including variants */
<div class="scrollbar-hide overflow-y-auto">
<input class="focus:focus-ring">

Custom variants: @variant

/* Define a variant that activates when a parent has a class */
@variant scrolled (&:where(.scrolled, .scrolled *));
@variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *));     /* class-based dark mode */
@variant rtl ([dir=rtl] &);                  /* RTL language support */

/* Usage */
<nav class="bg-transparent scrolled:bg-white/90 scrolled:shadow-sm">

Official plugins: @plugin

@import "tailwindcss";
@plugin "@tailwindcss/forms";       /* better default form styles */
@plugin "@tailwindcss/typography";  /* .prose for rich text rendering */

v3 → v4 quick reference

If you join a project migrating from v3, this table translates the old patterns:

v3 tailwind.config.js                →  v4 CSS equivalent
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
theme.extend.colors.brand: '#...'    →  @theme { --color-brand: oklch(...); }
theme.extend.fontFamily.display: [] →  @theme { --font-display: "..."; }
theme.extend.spacing[18]: '4.5rem'  →  @theme { --spacing-18: 4.5rem; }
theme.extend.screens[3xl]: '1920px' →  @theme { --breakpoint-3xl: 1920px; }
plug: require('@tailwindcss/forms')  →  @plugin "@tailwindcss/forms";
darkMode: 'class'                    →  @variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *));
addUtilities({ .foo: { ... } })      →  @utility foo { ... }
content: [...]                       →  (removed — automatic detection)

Solomon: "The config is not a file you set once and forget. It is where every design commitment is recorded — in the same language as the rest of your styles. Consult it before reaching for an arbitrary value."

questions.questionHtml: In Tailwind v4, where does configuration live — and what format does it take?
options: In your CSS file, inside an @theme {} block using CSS custom property syntax
In tailwind.config.js using a JavaScript export default object
In a .tailwindrc JSON file at the project root
In package.json under a 'tailwind' key
questions.correctAnswer: In your CSS file, inside an @theme {} block using CSS custom property syntax
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind v4 moved to CSS-first configuration. You define tokens inside @theme { --color-brand: ...; --spacing-18: 4.5rem; } in your CSS file. There is no tailwind.config.js. The naming convention --{category}-{name} tells Tailwind which utilities to generate.

questions.questionHtml: You add --color-brand-600: oklch(0.55 0.20 270) to your @theme block. Which Tailwind utilities are automatically generated?
options: bg-brand-600, text-brand-600, border-brand-600, ring-brand-600 — and every other colour utility variant
Only bg-brand-600 — other utilities require separate declarations
bg-brand-600 and text-brand-600 only — border utilities need explicit config
A CSS variable is created but no utility is generated automatically
questions.correctAnswer: bg-brand-600, text-brand-600, border-brand-600, ring-brand-600 — and every other colour utility variant
questions.explanationHtml: Every token in @theme automatically generates the full utility lattice for its category. A --color-* token becomes bg-*, text-*, border-*, ring-*, fill-*, stroke-*, and every other colour utility — plus opacity modifier support (e.g. bg-brand-600/50) for free.

questions.questionHtml: You need a custom spacing value of 4.5rem that you'll use frequently as padding, margin, and width. How do you define it in Tailwind v4?
options: @theme { --spacing-18: 4.5rem; } — generates p-18, m-18, w-18 automatically
As an arbitrary value p-[4.5rem] wherever needed
In a global CSS variable and use it with @apply
theme.extend.spacing['18'] in tailwind.config.js
questions.correctAnswer: @theme { --spacing-18: 4.5rem; } — generates p-18, m-18, w-18 automatically
questions.explanationHtml: In v4, adding --spacing-18: 4.5rem to @theme makes p-18, m-18, w-18, gap-18, and all other spacing utilities available at 4.5rem. Arbitrary values (p-[4.5rem]) are for genuine one-offs — values you use only once. Repeated values belong in @theme.

questions.questionHtml: You want to define a custom CSS utility class .scrollbar-hide that participates correctly in Tailwind v4's class system. Which approach is correct?
options: @utility scrollbar-hide { scrollbar-width: none; &::-webkit-scrollbar { display: none; } }
Add .scrollbar-hide to a regular CSS rule in index.css
theme.extend.utilities['scrollbar-hide'] in tailwind.config.js
@layer components { .scrollbar-hide { ... } }
questions.correctAnswer: @utility scrollbar-hide { scrollbar-width: none; &::-webkit-scrollbar { display: none; } }
questions.explanationHtml: @utility is the v4 way to define custom utility classes. Unlike a plain CSS rule or @layer components, a @utility participates in Tailwind's class system with correct specificity and variant support — so hover:scrollbar-hide or md:scrollbar-hide work automatically.

questions.questionHtml: A startup built their product using raw colour utilities (text-indigo-600, bg-indigo-500) across 300 files. Marketing wants the brand colour changed to teal. A developer says it's a "quick find-and-replace." A senior engineer disagrees. Who is right, and what architectural choice would have made this a 5-minute change?
questions.correctAnswer: The senior is right — find-and-replace is fragile and conflates brand intent with any use of indigo. The correct approach was semantic tokens: define --color-brand-600 in @theme, use bg-brand-600 everywhere. A rebrand is then @theme { --color-brand-600: oklch(0.53 0.17 155); } — one line.
questions.explanationHtml: Without semantic tokens, every indigo class could mean 'brand' or 'decorative' — there is no way to tell. A find-and-replace will miss some and break others. With @theme { --color-brand-600: oklch(...); } and bg-brand-600 throughout, a rebrand is a single variable change. The utility classes never touch. This is the core value of the semantic token pattern.

subChunks.title: clsx, tailwind-merge, and CVA
subChunks.hookHtml: Knowing utility classes is the easy part. The hard part is wiring them to component logic — variants, props, overrides — without your JSX becoming an unreadable string of concatenated conditions. Three small libraries solve this completely, and every serious React + Tailwind codebase uses them.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Sable the Illuminator has arranged three crystal vials on Solomon's workbench. Each is small, almost overlooked beside the Archmage's thick tomes. But Sable's eyes are sharp.

Sable the Illuminator: "These three — clsx, tailwind-merge, class-variance-authority — are the entire authoring layer for Tailwind in React. Master them and your components become readable. Ignore them and you will be maintaining spaghetti string concatenation forever."

Problem 1: Complex conditional classes

String concatenation works but becomes unreadable fast:

// Readable now, nightmare at 10 conditions
<button className={'px-4 py-2 rounded ' + (isPrimary ? 'bg-blue-600 text-white' : 'bg-gray-100 text-gray-700') + (isDisabled ? ' opacity-50 cursor-not-allowed' : '')}>

clsx is the solution. It accepts strings, objects, and arrays, filtering out falsy values:

import { clsx } from 'clsx';

// Strings
clsx('px-4 py-2', 'rounded')  // → 'px-4 py-2 rounded'

// Conditional expressions
clsx('px-4 py-2', isActive && 'bg-blue-600', isDisabled && 'opacity-50')
// → 'px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600'  (if active, not disabled)

// Object syntax (key = class, value = condition)
clsx('px-4 py-2', {
  'bg-blue-600 text-white': isPrimary,
  'bg-gray-100 text-gray-700': !isPrimary,
  'opacity-50 cursor-not-allowed': isDisabled,
})

// Arrays are flattened
clsx(['px-4 py-2', isActive && 'ring-2'])

Problem 2: Tailwind class conflicts when merging

Here is the subtle but critical problem. If a parent component sets px-4 and a caller passes className="px-8", both classes end up on the element. Which wins depends on which one appears later in Tailwind's generated stylesheet — and that order is not guaranteed to match your mental model.

// Component internals
<button className={clsx('px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600', className)}>

// Caller passes
<MyButton className="px-8" />

// Result: class="px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 px-8"
// Which px wins? Depends on stylesheet order. Unpredictable.

tailwind-merge understands Tailwind's utility groups and resolves conflicts intelligently — the last class in the group wins:

import { twMerge } from 'tailwind-merge';

twMerge('px-4 py-2', 'px-8')     // → 'py-2 px-8'
twMerge('text-sm', 'text-lg')    // → 'text-lg'
twMerge('bg-red-500', 'bg-blue-600')  // → 'bg-blue-600'

// It understands related groups too:
twMerge('p-4', 'px-8')           // → 'p-4 px-8'  (px-8 overrides only x-axis)

The cn() pattern — combine both

This is the universal pattern. You will find it in every serious codebase, usually in lib/utils.ts:

// lib/utils.ts
import { clsx, type ClassValue } from 'clsx';
import { twMerge } from 'tailwind-merge';

export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
  return twMerge(clsx(inputs));
}

// Usage in any component:
<button
  className={cn(
    'px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 text-white rounded-md font-medium',  // base
    className,            // caller override — conflicts resolved by twMerge
    isDisabled && 'opacity-50 cursor-not-allowed',              // runtime condition
    isLoading && 'relative text-transparent',                   // another condition
  )}
>

class-variance-authority (CVA) — typed component variants

When a component has multiple variants (primary/secondary/ghost) and sizes (sm/md/lg), CVA gives you a typed, readable declaration instead of nested ternaries:

import { cva, type VariantProps } from 'class-variance-authority';

const button = cva(
  // Base classes applied to ALL variants
  'inline-flex items-center justify-center font-medium rounded-md transition-colors duration-150 focus-visible:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-offset-2 disabled:opacity-50 disabled:pointer-events-none',
  {
    variants: {
      variant: {
        primary:     'bg-blue-600 text-white hover:bg-blue-700 focus-visible:ring-blue-500',
        secondary:   'bg-white text-gray-700 border border-gray-300 hover:bg-gray-50 focus-visible:ring-gray-400 shadow-sm',
        ghost:       'text-gray-700 hover:bg-gray-100 focus-visible:ring-gray-400',
        destructive: 'bg-red-600 text-white hover:bg-red-700 focus-visible:ring-red-500',
      },
      size: {
        sm: 'text-xs px-3 py-1.5 gap-1.5',
        md: 'text-sm px-4 py-2 gap-2',
        lg: 'text-base px-6 py-3 gap-2.5',
      },
    },
    defaultVariants: { variant: 'primary', size: 'md' },
  }
);

// TypeScript type for the variant props:
type ButtonProps = VariantProps<typeof button> & React.ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement> & {
  className?: string;
};

function Button({ variant, size, className, ...props }: ButtonProps) {
  return <button className={cn(button({ variant, size }), className)} {...props} />;
}

// Usage — fully typed, IntelliSense shows all options:
<Button variant="secondary" size="lg">Cancel</Button>
<Button variant="destructive">Delete account</Button>

Sable: "This is how Shadcn/ui builds every component. The variant declaration is the component's contract. It's not just a style choice — it's a typed API."

CVA shines in compound components too. An IconButton can compose the button variant, adding an icon variant on top without duplicating base classes.

questions.questionHtml: What does twMerge('px-4 py-2', 'px-8') return?
options: 'py-2 px-8'
'px-4 py-2 px-8'
'px-4 py-2'
'px-8 py-2 px-4'
questions.correctAnswer: 'py-2 px-8'
questions.explanationHtml: tailwind-merge understands that px-4 and px-8 are in the same utility group. The later value (px-8) wins and px-4 is dropped.

questions.questionHtml: What is the purpose of class-variance-authority (CVA)?
options: Declaring component variants in a typed, structured way that generates the correct class strings
Automatically resolving conflicting Tailwind utilities
Generating CSS variables from your config
Purging unused classes from the build output
questions.correctAnswer: Declaring component variants in a typed, structured way that generates the correct class strings
questions.explanationHtml: CVA takes a base class string and a variants object, returns a function that maps variant props to final class strings, and exposes TypeScript types for those props via VariantProps.

questions.questionHtml: A component applies className={cn('text-sm font-medium', props.className)}. A caller passes className="text-lg font-bold". What is the final resolved class string?
options: 'font-bold text-lg'
'text-sm font-medium text-lg font-bold'
'text-sm font-medium'
'text-lg font-medium'
questions.correctAnswer: 'font-bold text-lg'
questions.explanationHtml: tailwind-merge (via cn) resolves both text-sm/text-lg and font-medium/font-bold conflicts. The caller's classes win, producing font-bold text-lg.

questions.questionHtml: Which syntax is correct for using clsx to conditionally add a class?
options: clsx('base', isActive && 'bg-blue-600')
clsx('base', isActive ? true : 'bg-blue-600')
clsx('base' + isActive + 'bg-blue-600')
clsx('base', [isActive, 'bg-blue-600'])
questions.correctAnswer: clsx('base', isActive && 'bg-blue-600')
questions.explanationHtml: clsx filters out falsy values. When isActive is false, false && 'bg-blue-600' evaluates to false, which clsx ignores. When true, it evaluates to 'bg-blue-600', which clsx includes.

questions.questionHtml: A team reviews a PR. A junior built a button component with 12 variants using nested ternaries: variant === 'primary' ? 'bg-blue-600 ...' : variant === 'secondary' ? 'bg-white ...' : .... A senior asks them to rewrite it. What tool should they use, and what specific advantage does it give over ternaries besides readability?
questions.correctAnswer: CVA (class-variance-authority). Beyond readability, CVA exposes TypeScript types via VariantProps automatically, so callers get IntelliSense for valid variant values and TypeScript errors on invalid ones. The ternary approach has no types.
questions.explanationHtml: Nested ternaries are not typed — TypeScript cannot infer which strings are valid variant values. CVA's VariantProps<typeof buttonVariants> gives the component a proper typed API, catches typos at compile time, and documents the variant contract in one place.

subChunks.title: Accessibility with Tailwind
subChunks.hookHtml: Accessibility is not optional — it is a legal requirement under WCAG, the ADA, and the European Accessibility Act, and it is a professional expectation at every serious company. Tailwind gives you all the tools. Using them correctly is the mark of an expert.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Lyra the Scribe leads you down a spiral staircase to a room lit by a single lamp. A blindfolded figure sits at the desk, tracing a page with her fingertips. Lyra speaks quietly.

Lyra the Scribe: "A spell that works only for some readers is a spell half-cast. Let me show you the five habits that cover ninety percent of accessibility work in a Tailwind codebase."

Habit 1: focus-visible: over focus:

This is the single most common accessibility mistake in Tailwind projects.

// ❌ WRONG — shows a ring on every mouse click (annoying)
<button class="focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500">Save</button>

// ✅ CORRECT — ring appears only when focused via keyboard
<button class="focus:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500 focus-visible:ring-offset-2">Save</button>

focus-visible: maps to :focus-visible — a CSS pseudo-class the browser only applies when it believes focus came from the keyboard, not a mouse click. This is what designers mean when they say "remove the focus outline" — they mean for mouse users. Keyboard users still need it, and removing it entirely is a WCAG violation.

Habit 2: sr-only for icon-only controls

Every icon-only button must have a text label for screen readers:

<button class="p-2 rounded-md focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" class="w-5 h-5" />
  <span class="sr-only">Close dialog</span>
</button>

<!-- sr-only equivalent CSS (what Tailwind generates): -->
.sr-only {
  position: absolute;
  width: 1px; height: 1px;
  padding: 0; margin: -1px;
  overflow: hidden;
  clip: rect(0,0,0,0);
  white-space: nowrap;
  border-width: 0;
}

The text is invisible on screen but announced by screen readers. Always mark SVG icons with aria-hidden="true" to prevent them being read aloud as noise.

Habit 3: ARIA state variants (Tailwind v3.2+)

Style from accessible state rather than toggling classes with JavaScript:

<!-- Chevron that rotates when dropdown opens -->
<button aria-expanded="false" class="flex items-center gap-2">
  Menu
  <svg class="w-4 h-4 transition-transform aria-expanded:rotate-180" />
</button>

<!-- Tab that shows active state -->
<button role="tab" aria-selected="false"
  class="px-4 py-2 text-sm border-b-2 border-transparent
         aria-selected:border-blue-600 aria-selected:text-blue-600 aria-selected:font-medium">
  Overview
</button>

<!-- Disabled state via aria -->
<button aria-disabled="true"
  class="px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 text-white aria-disabled:opacity-50 aria-disabled:cursor-not-allowed">
  Submit
</button>

This pattern keeps your ARIA attributes as the single source of truth for state. JS toggles the ARIA attribute; CSS responds to it. Cleaner than parallel class-and-attribute management.

Habit 4: Colour contrast

WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal body text and 3:1 for large text (18px+ or 14px+ bold). Several popular combinations fail:

// Contrast ratios against white background:
gray-400:   3.5:1  ❌ fails for body text
gray-500:   4.6:1  ✓ barely passes — prefer gray-600
gray-600:   5.9:1  ✓ solid
gray-700:   8.6:1  ✓ strong
slate-500:  4.6:1  ✓ barely — prefer slate-600 (6.9:1)
blue-400:   2.5:1  ❌ use blue-700 (5.5:1) for text on white

Use browser DevTools accessibility panel or webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/ before shipping any custom colour pairing.

Habit 5: Reduced motion

<div class="animate-bounce motion-reduce:animate-none">
<div class="transition-transform duration-300 motion-reduce:transition-none">

Users with vestibular disorders can be physically harmed by excessive motion. motion-reduce: maps to prefers-reduced-motion: reduce. Add it to every animated element — it costs nothing and can mean a great deal to someone.

Lyra: "Five habits. Write them on the wall above your desk. Every component you ship should pass all five before it leaves your branch."

subChunks.title: Performance and the JIT Scanner
subChunks.hookHtml: Tailwind's scanner is the reason production CSS stays tiny. It only emits the classes you actually use. But it learns what you use by scanning source files as plain text — not by executing your code. Understanding this distinction prevents the most common production bug in every Tailwind codebase, regardless of version.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Master Ember places a thin book titled The Scanner on the workbench. He does not open it.

Master Ember: "Tailwind's great virtue is that it emits nothing you do not use. Its great trap is that it decides what you use by reading your source files as text — not executing them. Tailwind v4 removed the content array. The scanning rule itself did not change."

How the scanner works in v4

Tailwind v4 automatically detects your project files — no content array required. At build time (and during HMR), it reads all relevant source files, looks for strings that match utility patterns, and emits only those utilities. It does this with text matching — no JavaScript execution, no static analysis.

For edge cases, you can explicitly tell the scanner where to look:

/* index.css */
@import "tailwindcss";

/* ✅ Include a component library in node_modules */
@source "../node_modules/@my-org/ui/src/**/*.tsx";

/* ❌ Never include your own compiled CSS — circular scan: */
/* @source "../dist/**/*.css" */

The dynamic class trap — the #1 production bug

Always manifests the same way: works in development, wrong in production. The scanner sees fragments, not complete class strings.

// ❌ BROKEN — 'text-red-500' and 'text-green-500' never appear as
// complete strings. Only 'text-' and '-500' are in source.
const statusClass = `text-${status === 'error' ? 'red' : 'green'}-500`;
<p className={statusClass}>{message}</p>

// In dev: may still render (HMR keeps a broader set).
// In production: scanner never found these classes. No CSS emitted.

// ✅ CORRECT — complete strings are visible in source
const statusClasses = {
  error:   'text-red-500',
  success: 'text-green-500',
  warning: 'text-yellow-500',
  info:    'text-blue-500',
};
<p className={statusClasses[status] ?? 'text-gray-500'}>{message}</p>

The rule is absolute: never construct a Tailwind class by interpolating a fragment of it. The full class string must appear verbatim in a scanned file.

Safelisting — for classes from external data

When class names come from a CMS, database, or API and cannot appear verbatim in source, use @source inline() in your CSS:

/* Safelist exact classes */
@source inline("text-red-500 text-green-500 bg-red-100 bg-green-100");

/* Pattern syntax — generates a family of classes */
@source inline("{bg,text}-{red,green,blue,yellow}-{100,500,900}");

/* Variant support — include with responsive or state prefixes */
@source inline("hover:bg-{red,green,blue}-500");

Use safelisting sparingly — it bypasses scanning and bloats your bundle if patterns are too broad.

Checking your bundle size

After npm run build, inspect dist/assets/*.css. A well-built Tailwind app for medium complexity is typically 8–25 KB gzipped. Red flags:

  • 100+ KB: an @source path is matching node_modules broadly or a large JSON data file
  • Styles missing in prod but present in dev: dynamic class interpolation bug
  • Styles present but unneeded: @source inline() pattern is too broad

Arbitrary values — when they are and aren't appropriate

// ✅ Appropriate — one-off pixel-perfect value from a design spec
<div class="top-[57px]">  // navbar is exactly 57px — no token exists

// ❌ Not appropriate — value used in 15 places
<div class="mt-[17px]">   // add --spacing-4.25: 17px to @theme instead

// ✅ Appropriate — CSS expressions not available as a token
<div class="w-[calc(100%-4rem)]">

Ember: "Arbitrary values are an escape hatch, not a shortcut. When you see them accumulating, the @theme config is failing to represent the design system."

questions.questionHtml: In Tailwind v4, how do you safelist class names that come from a CMS or API and cannot appear verbatim in source?

questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind v4's automatic detection scans your project files but deliberately excludes node_modules for performance. For a component library that uses Tailwind classes in its source, add an explicit @source directive in your CSS. Never include your own compiled CSS output — that creates a circular scan.

questions.questionHtml: After a production build, the CSS file is 180 KB gzipped. What is the most likely cause?

questions.explanationHtml: When an @source path covers files with thousands of random strings that happen to match Tailwind patterns — like a large JSON data file or a broad node_modules/** glob — the scanner emits a utility for every match. A well-built medium-complexity Tailwind app should be 8–25 KB gzipped.

questions.questionHtml: A developer builds a status feed where post categories are fetched from an API. They write className={`bg-${post.category}-100 text-${post.category}-800`}. It works in development. After deploying to production, all category badges show no background colour. Explain what happened and give two valid fixes.
questions.correctAnswer: The scanner saw only fragments ('bg-' and '-100'), never a complete class string. In production those utilities were not emitted. Fix 1: a lookup object mapping each category to its complete class strings. Fix 2: @source inline("{bg,text}-{news,sport,tech}-{100,800}") in the CSS file.
questions.explanationHtml: Dev mode has a broader initial compilation, masking the bug. The production scanner is strict — only emit what was found as a complete string. The lookup-object approach is cleanest (handles future categories explicitly). @source inline() is appropriate when the category list is short and known, or when class names truly come from external data at runtime.

subChunks.title: Design Systems and Shadcn/ui
subChunks.hookHtml: Most production React + Tailwind apps don't build every component from scratch. Understanding how Shadcn/ui works — and why it's designed the way it is — teaches you the entire component-library architecture that underlies nearly every serious codebase you'll join in 2024 and beyond.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Grand Archmage Solomon closes the config scrolls and opens a slim codex with a dark cover. On the spine: Shadcn.

Grand Archmage Solomon: "Most students see a component library and ask: 'How do I install it?' The question that reveals mastery is: 'How is it built?' Because once you can read a Shadcn component, you can modify it, extend it, or replace it — and you'll never be held hostage by an upstream package again."

What Shadcn/ui is — and isn't

Shadcn/ui is not a traditional component library you install as a dependency. You run a CLI command and it copies component source code into your project. You own it entirely. This is intentional.

npx shadcn-ui@latest add button
# Creates: components/ui/button.tsx in YOUR project
# You can open it, read it, and change every class.

Architecture: Radix UI (accessible, unstyled primitives) + Tailwind CSS (styling) + CVA (variants) + cn() (merging).

Reading a Shadcn component

// components/ui/button.tsx (Shadcn-generated — now in YOUR project)
import { Slot } from '@radix-ui/react-slot';
import { cva, type VariantProps } from 'class-variance-authority';
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils';

const buttonVariants = cva(
  // Base: accessibility, transitions, disabled state all baked in
  'inline-flex items-center justify-center rounded-md text-sm font-medium ring-offset-background transition-colors focus-visible:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring focus-visible:ring-offset-2 disabled:pointer-events-none disabled:opacity-50',
  {
    variants: {
      variant: {
        default:     'bg-primary text-primary-foreground hover:bg-primary/90',
        destructive: 'bg-destructive text-destructive-foreground hover:bg-destructive/90',
        outline:     'border border-input bg-background hover:bg-accent hover:text-accent-foreground',
        secondary:   'bg-secondary text-secondary-foreground hover:bg-secondary/80',
        ghost:       'hover:bg-accent hover:text-accent-foreground',
        link:        'text-primary underline-offset-4 hover:underline',
      },
      size: {
        default: 'h-10 px-4 py-2',
        sm:      'h-9 rounded-md px-3',
        lg:      'h-11 rounded-md px-8',
        icon:    'h-10 w-10',
      },
    },
    defaultVariants: { variant: 'default', size: 'default' },
  }
);

interface ButtonProps
  extends React.ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement>,
    VariantProps<typeof buttonVariants> {
  asChild?: boolean;
}

const Button = React.forwardRef<HTMLButtonElement, ButtonProps>(
  ({ className, variant, size, asChild = false, ...props }, ref) => {
    const Comp = asChild ? Slot : 'button';
    return (
      <Comp
        className={cn(buttonVariants({ variant, size, className }))}
        ref={ref}
        {...props}
      />
    );
  }
);

Notice the CSS variables: bg-primary, text-primary-foreground, bg-destructive. These are not Tailwind built-ins — they are defined in globals.css:

/* globals.css — Shadcn theming layer */
:root {
  --background: 0 0% 100%;
  --foreground: 222.2 84% 4.9%;
  --primary: 222.2 47.4% 11.2%;
  --primary-foreground: 210 40% 98%;
  --secondary: 210 40% 96.1%;
  --secondary-foreground: 222.2 47.4% 11.2%;
  --destructive: 0 84.2% 60.2%;
  --destructive-foreground: 210 40% 98%;
  --ring: 222.2 84% 4.9%;
}

.dark {
  --background: 222.2 84% 4.9%;
  --foreground: 210 40% 98%;
  --primary: 210 40% 98%;
  --primary-foreground: 222.2 47.4% 11.2%;
}

/* tailwind.config.js wires them in: */
theme: {
  extend: {
    colors: {
      primary: { DEFAULT: 'hsl(var(--primary))', foreground: 'hsl(var(--primary-foreground))' },
    }
  }
}

When to use Shadcn vs build from scratch

  • Use Shadcn/Radix: Dialog, Select, Dropdown Menu, Toast, Command (search), Tooltip, Tabs, Accordion — anything with ARIA roles, focus management, or keyboard navigation. These are genuinely hard to implement correctly.
  • Build from scratch: Card, Badge, Divider, Skeleton, Avatar — simple visual components with no interactive behaviour. They don't need Radix; a few Tailwind classes is all they need.

The rule: if a component needs role, aria-* attributes, or keyboard event handling to be correct, use a primitive. Don't reinvent focus traps.

Solomon: "When you copy a Shadcn component into your project, you are not accepting a dependency — you are accepting responsibility. Read every line. Understand every class. Then it is yours."

questions.questionHtml: A team is building a custom dropdown menu. A junior suggests building it from scratch with Tailwind. A senior says to use Radix UI's DropdownMenu primitive and style it with Tailwind. The junior says they're the same amount of work. Who is right?

questions.questionHtml: Six months after adding Shadcn to a project, a developer finds a bug in the Shadcn Dialog component — it doesn't correctly restore focus to the trigger element on close. They check the Shadcn GitHub and see it was fixed two weeks ago. How do they get the fix, and how does this differ from fixing a bug in Material UI?
questions.correctAnswer: Since Shadcn source lives in their project, they manually apply the fix — copy the relevant code change from the Shadcn GitHub diff into their components/ui/dialog.tsx. With Material UI (a package), they would run npm update. Shadcn's tradeoff: full control and no forced upgrades, but manual maintenance. Material UI's tradeoff: easy updates, but cannot modify internals.
questions.explanationHtml: This is the core Shadcn tradeoff. Owning the source means no version lock-in and full customisation, but it also means manually tracking upstream fixes. Teams should decide deliberately whether the trade is worth it for their project size and maintenance capacity.

Pattern 4: Footer

<footer class="bg-gray-900 text-gray-400 py-12">

    <div>
      <p class="text-white font-semibold mb-1">Your Name</p>
      <p class="text-sm">Full-Stack Developer — Available for contract work</p>
    </div>
    <div class="flex gap-6">
      <a href="https://github.com" class="text-sm hover:text-white transition-colors">GitHub</a>
      <a href="https://linkedin.com" class="text-sm hover:text-white transition-colors">LinkedIn</a>
      <a href="mailto:you@email.com" class="text-sm hover:text-white transition-colors">Email</a>
    </div>
  </div>
</footer>

How to approach a new portfolio project

  1. Start mobile-first. Design and code for the smallest breakpoint first. Breakpoint prefixes add to it.
  2. Establish a type hierarchy first. Decide your h1 (text-5xl), h2 (text-3xl), h3 (text-xl), body (text-base) before writing a single other class.
  3. Pick one accent colour and use three shades. light/100 for backgrounds, mid/600 for text, dark/900 for high-contrast. Avoid more than two accent colours.
  4. Use container mx-auto px-4 on every section wrapper. Never apply width constraints inside sections.
  5. Add transition-* to everything interactive from day one. Retrofitting animations is painful.
  6. Use group + group-hover: for card hover effects. This keeps hover logic on one element even when children need to respond.

questions.questionHtml: Which pair of classes creates a fixed navbar that has a frosted-glass effect over content below it?

questions.questionHtml: You have a project card where hovering the card should scale the card image. Which pattern correctly applies the scale only to the image, triggered by hovering the card?
options: Add class 'group' to the card, then 'group-hover:scale-105 transition-transform' to the image
Add 'hover:scale-105' to both the card and the image
Add 'hover:*:scale-105' to the card to target all children
Use JavaScript to add 'scale-105' to the image on card mouseenter
questions.correctAnswer: Add class 'group' to the card, then 'group-hover:scale-105 transition-transform' to the image
questions.explanationHtml: The group class marks the parent. Any descendant with a group-hover: prefix applies that utility when the group ancestor is hovered. This keeps the hover trigger and the visual response cleanly separated without JavaScript.

bg-blue-100 text-blue-800 rounded px-2 py-1 text-xs
border-2 border-blue-500 text-blue-500 rounded-full px-3
bg-transparent outline outline-blue-400 text-blue-400 rounded-full

questions.explanationHtml: The /20 opacity modifier on bg-blue-500 creates a 20% opaque blue background — the translucent effect. text-blue-400 is light enough to look good on a dark hero background. rounded-full produces the pill shape.

questions.questionHtml: A junior developer's portfolio hero section looks perfect on their 1440px laptop but the text is illegible on a 375px phone — the heading is 72px and overflows the screen. They ask what responsive prefix to add. What do you tell them, and what underlying principle did they miss when building it?
questions.correctAnswer: They should rewrite it mobile-first: start with text-4xl or text-3xl (legible on phone), then add md:text-5xl lg:text-7xl. The principle they missed: unprefixed utilities are the base (smallest screen). They built desktop-first and tried to 'fix' mobile with prefixes — but there is no max-width prefix to undo a large base size. Mobile-first means the base is the smallest. Larger screens add, never subtract.
questions.explanationHtml: There is no Tailwind equivalent of a 'max-sm:' prefix to decrease font size at small screens (it exists but is rarely idiomatic). The correct pattern is always to set the smallest-screen value as the base and override upward. Once this principle is internalised, responsive design becomes additive composition rather than defensive overriding.

subChunks.title: Design Handoff: Figma to Tailwind
subChunks.hookHtml: Knowing Tailwind classes is necessary. Translating a Figma design into those classes fluently is what makes you useful on day one of a real job. Most junior developers struggle at this seam — not because they don't know Tailwind, but because they've never practised reading a spec.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Solomon sets a printed screenshot on the desk beside a Figma URL. No class list. No starter code.

Grand Archmage Solomon: "Every real project starts here: a design, and a blank editor. The designer has made decisions about spacing, colour, type, and layout. Your job is to read those decisions correctly and express them in Tailwind. That is a skill. It requires practice."

Reading spacing from a design

Figma Dev Mode shows computed values directly. Without it, you measure by eye and snap to the nearest token:

  • Padding inside a component — hover the inner element in Figma, read the spacing values. Map to the Tailwind scale: 8px → p-2, 12px → p-3, 16px → p-4, 24px → p-6.
  • Gap between elements — select both elements, read the gap. If it's 16px between two items in a row → gap-4 on the flex parent.
  • Margins — outer spacing between sections is usually larger: 32px → my-8, 48px → my-12, 64px → my-16.

When in doubt, round to the nearest token. A 14px padding is more likely intentional p-3.5 than a design accident. An 18px margin is almost certainly m-4 with an off-by-one in the design.

Reading typography

  • Font size — 12px → text-xs, 14px → text-sm, 16px → text-base, 18px → text-lg, 20px → text-xl, 24px → text-2xl.
  • Font weight — read the weight number from Figma: 400 → font-normal, 500 → font-medium, 600 → font-semibold, 700 → font-bold.
  • Line height — Figma shows as a pixel or percentage value. 150% on 16px body text → 24px line height → leading-normal (1.5). 125% on a heading → leading-tight.
  • Letter spacing — small positive values (0.5–1px on small caps labels) → tracking-wide or tracking-wider.

Reading colour

There are two scenarios:

Scenario A — the project uses Tailwind's default palette. Copy the hex from Figma and look it up in the Tailwind colour reference. #6366f1 is indigo-500. #374151 is gray-700. Memorising the gray scale (see tw-a4) pays off here.

Scenario B — the project has a custom palette. The colours will be defined in @theme as semantic tokens. Don't hardcode hex values — use the token name. Ask a senior developer or check the design system documentation.

Reading layout

  • Row of items — flex. Check if they're evenly spaced → justify-between, or packed left → justify-start gap-4.
  • Grid of cards — grid. Count columns per row. Mobile: 1 col, tablet: 2 cols, desktop: 3 or 4 cols → grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3.
  • Sidebar + content — grid with fixed sidebar: grid-cols-[240px_1fr].
  • Centred column — max-w-* + mx-auto + px-* for side padding.

The professional workflow

  1. Identify the components — before writing any code, mentally group the design into components: nav, hero, card, footer. Plan the order.
  2. Mobile-first — start with the phone layout. Add breakpoint prefixes for larger screens.
  3. Structure before colour — get the layout and spacing correct first. Add colours, shadows, and decorative classes last.
  4. Closest token wins — always prefer a Tailwind token over an arbitrary value. If you're using more than 2–3 arbitrary values on a component, the @theme config is missing those tokens.
  5. Check in the browser at multiple sizes — designs are static; browsers are dynamic. Resize constantly.

Solomon: "The developer who can read a design accurately, and translate it faithfully the first time, will always be valued above the one who must be corrected six times before the spacing is right. Train this skill deliberately."

questions.questionHtml: A Figma component shows 16px padding on all sides and 8px gap between child elements in a row. Which Tailwind classes represent these values?
options: p-4 on the container, gap-2 on the flex parent
p-16 on the container, gap-8 on the flex parent
padding-4 on the container, flex-gap-2 on the parent
p-4 on the container, space-x-2 on each child
questions.correctAnswer: p-4 on the container, gap-2 on the flex parent
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind's 4px base unit: 16px = 4 × 4px → p-4. 8px gap = 2 × 4px → gap-2 on the flex or grid parent. Memorising the core scale (4→1, 8→2, 12→3, 16→4, 24→6, 32→8) is a prerequisite skill for design handoff.

questions.questionHtml: A Figma text element shows: size 14px, weight 600, line-height 20px. Which Tailwind class combination is correct?
options: text-sm font-semibold leading-5
text-14 font-600 leading-20
text-sm font-bold leading-relaxed
font-size-sm weight-semibold line-5
questions.correctAnswer: text-sm font-semibold leading-5
questions.explanationHtml: 14px → text-sm. Weight 600 → font-semibold. Leading-5 = 1.25rem = 20px — the exact pixel value. Tailwind's leading utilities use the same numbering as the spacing scale: leading-5 = 5 × 4px = 20px. When Figma gives you a pixel line-height, map it to the nearest leading value.

questions.questionHtml: A Figma card has 18px internal padding. There is no p-4.5 in standard Tailwind. What is the correct approach?
options: Use p-[18px] for a one-off value, or add --spacing-4.5: 18px to @theme if used repeatedly
Round to p-4 (16px) — Tailwind always rounds down
Use p-5 (20px) — Tailwind always rounds up
Use p-4 and fix the design to 16px — non-scale values should not exist
questions.correctAnswer: Use p-[18px] for a one-off value, or add --spacing-4.5: 18px to @theme if used repeatedly
questions.explanationHtml: When a design value falls between scale tokens, Tailwind's arbitrary value syntax (p-[18px]) is the correct one-off fix. If the same value appears throughout the design, it signals a token gap — add it to @theme as --spacing-4.5: 18px, which generates p-4.5, m-4.5, etc. Silently rounding to a nearby value will cause the implementation to differ visibly from the design.

questions.questionHtml: The Figma spec shows the card header as: logo on the left, nav links in the centre, a CTA button on the right — all vertically centred. What is the correct Tailwind layout?
options: flex items-center on the header — then justify-between or a spacer div to push content to edges
grid grid-cols-3 place-items-center on the header
flex flex-col items-center on the header
relative positioning on each child with absolute left/right
questions.correctAnswer: flex items-center on the header — then justify-between or a spacer div to push content to edges
questions.explanationHtml: A horizontal row of vertically-centred items is the canonical flex use case: flex items-center. To push the logo left and the CTA right with links in the middle, the most common patterns are: justify-between on the container (works when there are exactly two or three items), or a flex-1 spacer div between the logo group and the CTA group. Grid is overpowered for this and position-absolute requires removing elements from flow.

questions.questionHtml: A developer receives a Figma design for a pricing card. The card has: 32px top/bottom padding, 24px left/right padding, 8px rounded corners, a #6366f1 background colour, and white text. Their first attempt at the card uses bg-[#6366f1]. A senior developer reviews it and asks them to change one thing. What is it, and why?
questions.correctAnswer: Replace bg-[#6366f1] with bg-indigo-500 (or the project's semantic token bg-primary). #6366f1 is Tailwind's exact indigo-500. Using the arbitrary hex hardcodes a value that should come from the design system — if the brand colour changes, bg-indigo-500 can be updated at the @theme level while bg-[#6366f1] stays broken.
questions.explanationHtml: #6366f1 is the default Tailwind indigo-500. Using bg-indigo-500 (or a semantic token like bg-primary) means the colour participates in the design system — it can be updated in one place. Arbitrary hex values are invisible to the theming layer: they will not update when someone adjusts the brand colour token, and they make the intent of the colour opaque to future developers.
